newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Dogs join protests in Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Dogs join protests in Serbia.

text.p: Serbia's colourful protest movement trotted out a new strategy on Sunday, getting hundreds of pet dogs to walk -- and sometimes bark -- for democracy.
Hundreds of dogs joined their masters for a 63rd day of street protests against the ruling Socialists' annulment of opposition victories in municipal elections.
Great danes, bulldogs, poodles, cocker spaniels, Irish setters, rotweilers, dalmatians and chihuahuas added a canine cacophony to the usual din of whistles, drums and chants.
Some of the pooches looked flustered from all the racket while others joined in heartily, barking in unison at riot police trying to enforce a ban on street marches.
Nine weeks of demonstrations by Serbia's Zajedno (Together) coalition have been distinctive for non-violence, creativity and humour, and Sunday's rally of the dogs was no exception.
On Saturday, protesters dressed up in uniforms to mock the riot police who shadow them every day.
But autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic and his Socialist Party (SPS) have shown little sign of backing down from their cancellation of the municipal election results.

Daily rallies notwithstanding, Serbia's crisis looked set to drag on without resolution, barring strikes in support of Zajedno by traditionally pro-Socialist workers and farmers who have shunned the protest movement so far.

An OSCE investigation dismissed the Socialists' claim of unspecified "irregularities" in the elections and verified that Zajedno captured majorities in 14 major Serbian towns including the two biggest, Belgrade and Nis.

With the West warning Milosevic to respect democratic principles or forget about aid for Serbia's wrecked economy, Socialist-led electoral commissions admitted Zajedno victories in Belgrade and Nis last week.

Hardline Socialists lodged an appeal against the commission verdict in Nis but it was swiftly rejected by the municipal court. Heartened Zajedno activists said they would convene the new local assembly on January 27 as a result.
But the Socialists retained other avenues for legalistic obstruction and political sabotage through state-dominated higher courts and the mainstream media, analysts said.
They believe Milosevic is playing for time by withholding clear instructions to party disciples, giving hardliners free rein to manoeuvre to regain political advantage.

Renewed anti-Serb violence in the Albanian-majority province of Kosovo could be an opportunity for Milosevic to divert attention from the election problem and reassert the appeal of strong Socialist leadership.

State-run mainstream media jumped on allegations by the Serb Socialist mayor of Pristina in Kosovo that Zajedno was involved in a car bombing that gravely injured the Serb rector of the city's university last week.
In Belgrade, Zajedno condemned the bomb attack and denied any connection with it.

Another indication of hardline SPS sentiment was the failure of Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic to attend the weekend funeral of his counterpart in Montenegro, Serbia's tiny federal partner.
Montenegrin foreign minister Janko Jeknic, who died in a car crash on Friday, was an eminent career diplomat who helped Montenegro pursue pro-Western economic and political policies.
Analysts said the absence of Milutinovic reflected anger in Belgrade at Montenegrin calls for an election compromise with Zajedno to help end Yugoslavia's international isolation.

A third signal of diehard strength in the SPS was a retreat by deputy Serbian premier Ratko Markovic from a statement he made on January 11 that "genuine and complete" election results must be honoured in Serbia.
On Saturday, Markovic said electoral commissioners' subsequent decision to recognise Zajedno's victory in Belgrade was a "nightmare of legal nonsense, unlawfulness and error".
He said the commission was not competent to overturn prior court decisions, which favoured the SPS. The deadline for the SPS to appeal against the Belgrade ruling was Monday.
